passages.t: Ask the LORD for rain, not the idols
passages.happening:
‘Ask the LORD for rain in springtime; the LORD makes the storm clouds’ (verse 1), and he gives showers and crops. ‘For idols speak deceit and diviners see illusions; they tell false dreams and offer empty comfort’ (verse 2). So the people wander like sheep, oppressed for lack of a shepherd.

God's anger burns against the shepherds, and he will punish the leaders. He cares for his flock, the house of Judah, and will make them like his majestic war horse (verse 3). ‘The cornerstone will come from Judah, the tent peg from him, as well as the battle bow and every ruler together’ (verse 4). They will fight because the LORD is with them (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The spring rains filled out the grain before harvest. People were tempted to look to idols and diviners for rain, as their neighbors did. The chapter calls them back to the God who makes the clouds.

Shepherds was the common word for rulers. The people suffer because their leaders have failed them and their religious advisers have offered empty comfort.

The cornerstone, the tent peg and the battle bow are pictures of leaders who hold the community together. The cornerstone bears the weight of a building, and the tent peg holds a tent firm. God will raise such leaders from Judah itself.
passages.later: Jeremiah condemned the shepherds who scattered God's flock (Jeremiah 23:1-2). A psalm speaks of ‘The stone the builders rejected’ that ‘has become the cornerstone’ (Psalm 118:22).
passages.asks: The people looked to idols and diviners for comfort and were left like sheep without a shepherd. Ask where you go for comfort that cannot give it. And ask who you look to as a leader, and whether they lead you toward God.

passages.t: God whistles for his scattered people
passages.happening:
‘I will strengthen the house of Judah and save the house of Joseph’ (verse 6). God will bring them back because he has compassion on them, and it will be as though he had never rejected them. Ephraim will be glad, and their children will see it and rejoice in the LORD (verse 7).

‘I will whistle for them to gather, for I have redeemed them’ (verse 8). Though he scattered them among the nations, they will remember him in distant lands and return with their children (verse 9). He will bring them back from Egypt and gather them from Assyria, to Gilead and Lebanon, until there is no more room (verse 10). They will pass through the sea of distress, the pride of Assyria will be brought down, and they will walk in the LORD's name (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
The house of Joseph and Ephraim are names for the northern tribes, scattered by Assyria nearly two centuries before. The promise is not only for Judah. God will bring the north home too and reunite his divided people.

A shepherd whistled to call his flock. Egypt and Assyria were the old powers of slavery and exile, and passing through the sea recalls the exodus. The return is pictured as a new exodus.

Gilead and Lebanon were lands to the east and north, at the edges of Israel's old territory. The people will be so many that they need room. These are promises to the scattered people of that age, and they make no claim about any modern state or border.
passages.later: Isaiah promised that the LORD would gather the remnant ‘from Assyria, from Egypt’ (Isaiah 11:11). Hosea pictured the exiles coming home trembling from Egypt and Assyria (Hosea 11:11).
passages.asks: God whistles for his scattered people, and they remember him in distant lands. Ask whether you have drifted far from God, and whether you can hear him calling. And ask what it means that God promises to take back those he once sent away.
